{{Short description|Proof method}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''incompressibility method''' is a [[Mathematical proof|proof]] method like the [[probabilistic method]], the counting method or the [[pigeonhole principle]]. To prove that an object in a certain class (on average) satisfies a certain property, select an object of that class that is [[Incompressible string|incompressible]]. If it does not satisfy the property, it can be compressed by [[Computability theory|computable]] coding. Since it can be generally proven that almost all objects in a given class are incompressible, the argument demonstrates that almost all objects in the class have the property involved (not just the average). To select an incompressible object is ineffective, and cannot be done by a computer program. However, a simple counting argument usually shows that almost all objects of a given class can be compressed by only a few [[bit]]s (are incompressible).

==History==
The incompressibility method depends on an objective, fixed notion of incompressibility. Such a notion was provided by the [[Kolmogorov complexity]] theory, named for [[Andrey Kolmogorov]].<ref>[http://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=ppi&paperid=68&option_lang=eng  A. N. Kolmogorov, "Three approaches to the definition of the concept 'quantity of information', ''Probl. Peredachi Inf.'', 1:1 (1965), 3–11]</ref>

One of the first uses of the incompressibility method with Kolmogorov complexity in the theory of computation was to prove that the running time of a one-tape [[Turing machine]] is quadratic for accepting a palindromic language and [[sorting algorithm]]s require at least <math>n \log n</math> time to sort <math>n</math> items.<ref name="Pa">[http://www-wjp.cs.uni-saarland.de/publikationen/Pa79.pdf W. J. Paul, "Kolmogorov's complexity and lower bounds", pp 325–333 in: L. Budach Ed., ''Proc. 2nd Int. Conf. Fund. Comput. Theory'', 1979.]</ref> One of the early influential papers using the incompressibility method was published in 1980.<ref name="PSS">W. J. Paul, J. I. Seiferas, J. Simon, "An information-theoretic approach to time bounds for on-line computation" (preliminary version), ''Proc. 12th  ACM Symp. Theory Comput (STOC)'', 357–367, 1980. {{doi|10.1016/0022-0000(81)90009-X}}</ref> The method was applied to a number of fields, and its name was coined in a textbook.<ref name="LV">[https://books.google.com/books?hl=en&lr=&id=JvXiBwAAQBAJ&oi=fnd&pg=PR5&dq=vitanyi+Introduction M. Li, P. M. B. Vitanyi, ''An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications'', Springer, 1993, 1997, 2008, Chapter 6.]</ref>

==Applications==

===Number theory===
According to an [[Mathematical beauty|elegant]] [[Euclid]]ean proof, there is an infinite number of [[prime number]]s. [[Bernhard Riemann]] demonstrated that the number of primes less than a given number is connected with the 0s of the [[Riemann zeta function]]. [[Jacques Hadamard]] and [[Charles Jean de la Vallée-Poussin]] proved in 1896 that this
number of primes is [[Asymptotic analysis|asymptotic]] to <math>n/\ln n</math>; see [[Prime number theorem]] (use <math>\ln</math> for the [[natural logarithm]] and <math>\log</math> for the [[binary logarithm]]). Using the incompressibility method, [[G. J. Chaitin]] argued as follows:  Each <math>n</math> can be described by its [[Integer factorization|prime factorization]] <math>n= p_1^{n_1} \cdots p_k^{n_k}</math> (which is unique), where <math>p_1, \ldots , p_k</math> are the first <math>k</math> primes which are (at most) <math>n</math> and the [[Exponentiation|exponents]] (possibly) 0. Each exponent is (at most) <math>\log n</math>, and can be described by <math> \log \log n</math> bits. The description of <math>n</math> can be given in <math>k \log \log n</math> bits, provided we know the value of <math>\log \log n</math> (enabling one to [[Parsing|parse]] the consecutive blocks of exponents). To describe <math>\log \log n</math> requires only <math>\log \log \log n</math> bits. Using the incompressibility of most positive integers, for each <math>k>0</math> there is a positive integer <math>n</math> of binary length <math>l\approx \log n</math> which cannot be described in fewer than <math>l</math> bits. This shows that the number of primes, <math>\pi(n)</math>  less than <math>n</math>, satisfies
 
:<math>
\pi(n) \geq \frac{\log n}{\log \log n} -o(1).
</math>

A more-sophisticated approach attributed to Piotr Berman (present proof partially by [[John Tromp]]) describes every incompressible <math>n</math> by <math>k</math> and <math>n/p_k</math>, where <math>p_k</math> is the largest prime number dividing <math>n</math>. Since <math>n</math> is incompressible, the length of this description must exceed <math>\log n</math>. To parse the first block of the description <math>k</math> must be given in prefix form <math>P(k)=\log k +\log \log k +\log \varepsilon(k)</math>, where <math>\varepsilon(k)</math> is an arbitrary, small, positive function. Therefore, <math>\log p_k \leq P(k)</math>. Hence, <math>p_k \leq n_k</math> with <math>n_k=\varepsilon(k)k\log k</math> for a special sequence of values <math>n_1, n_2,  \ldots </math>. This shows that the expression below holds for this special sequence, and a [[simple extension]] shows that it holds for every <math>n >0</math>:

:<math>
\pi(n) \geq \frac n {\varepsilon(n)\log n}.
</math>

Both proofs are presented in more detail.<ref name="LV"/>

===Graph theory===
A [[labeled graph]] <math>G=(V,E)</math> with <math>n</math> nodes can be represented by a string <math>E(G)</math> of <math>{n \choose 2}</math> bits, where each bit indicates the presence (or absence) of an edge between the pair of nodes in that position. <math>K(G) \geq {n \choose 2}</math>, and the [[Degree (graph theory)|degree]] <math>d</math> of each vertex satisfies

:<math>
|d-n/2| = O\left(\sqrt{n \log n}\right).
</math>

To prove this by the incompressibility method, if the deviation is larger we can compress the description of <math>G</math> below <math>K(G)</math>; this provides the required contradiction. This theorem is required in a more complicated proof, where the incompressibility argument is used a number of times to show that the number of unlabeled graphs is

:<math>
\sim \frac{2^{n \choose 2}}{n!}.
</math><ref>H. M. Buhrman, M. Li, J. T. Tromp, P. M. B. Vitanyi, "Kolmogorov random graphs and the incompressibility method", ''SIAM J. Comput.'', 29:2(1999), 590–599. {{doi|10.1137/S0097539797327805}}</ref>

===Combinatorics===
A transitive [[tournament]] is a complete [[directed graph]], <math>G=(V,E)</math>; if <math>(i,j),(j,k) \in E</math>, <math>(i,k) \in E</math>. Consider the set of all transitive tournaments on <math>n</math> nodes. Since a tournament is a labeled, directed [[complete graph]], it can be encoded by a string <math>E(G)</math> of <math>{n \choose 2}</math> bits where each bit indicates the direction of the edge between the pair of nodes in that position. Using this encoding, every transitive tournament contains a transitive subtournament on (at least) <math>v(n)</math> vertices with

:<math>
v(n) \leq 1+ \lfloor 2 \log n \rfloor.
</math>

This was shown as the first problem.<ref>[http://www.maa.org/publications/maa-reviews/probabilistic-methods-in-combinatorics  P. Erdos, J. Spencer, ''Probabilistic methods in combinatorics'', Academic Press, 1974.]</ref> It is easily solved by the incompressibility method,<ref>M. Li, P. M. B. Vitanyi,  "Kolmogorov complexity arguments in combinatorics", ''J. Combinatorial Theory'', Series A, 66:2(1994), 226–236. {{doi|10.1016/0097-3165(94)90064-7}}</ref> as are the coin-weighing problem, the number of covering families and expected properties; for example, at least a fraction of <math>1-1/n</math> of all transitive tournaments on <math>n</math> vertices have transitive subtournaments on not more than <math>1+2\lceil2 \log n \rceil</math> vertices. <math>n</math> is large enough.

If a number of events are [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] (in [[probability theory]]) of one another, the probability that none of the events occur can be easily calculated. If the events are dependent, the problem becomes difficult. [[Lovász local lemma]]<ref>[http://www.cs.elte.hu/~lovasz/scans/LocalLem.pdf P. Erdős, L. Lovász, "Problems and results on 3-chromatic hypergraphs and some related questions", in A. Hajnal, R. Rado, and V. T. Sós, eds. ''Infinite and Finite Sets (to Paul Erdős on his 60th birthday)''. North-Holland. pp. 609–627.]</ref> is a principle that if events are mostly independent of one another and have an individually-small probability, there is a positive probability that none of them will occur.<ref>R. A. Moser, G. Tardos, "A constructive proof of the general lovász local lemma", ''Journal of the ACM (JACM)'', 2:57(2010), 11. {{doi|10.1145/1667053.1667060}}</ref> It was proven by the incompressibility method.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://blog.computationalcomplexity.org/2009/06/kolmogorov-complexity-proof-of-lov.html|first=Lance|last=Fortnow|author-link=Lance Fortnow|title=A Kolmogorov Complexity Proof of the Lovász Local Lemma|date=2 June 2009|work=Computational Complexity|access-date=2025-08-21}}</ref> Using the incompressibility method, several versions of [[Expander graph|expanders]] and superconcentrator graphs were shown to exist.<ref>U. Schoning, "Construction of expanders and superconcentrators using Kolmogorov complexity", ''Random Structures & Algorithms'', 17:1(2000), 64–77. {{doi|10.1002/1098-2418(200008)17:1<64::AID-RSA5>3.0.CO;2-3}}</ref>

===Topological combinatorics===

In the [[Heilbronn triangle problem]], throw <math>n</math> points in the [[unit square]] and determine the maximum of the minimal area of a triangle formed by three of the points over all possible arrangements. This problem was solved for small arrangements, and much work was done on asymptotic expression as a function of <math>n</math>. The original conjecture of [[Heilbronn]] was <math>O(1/n^2)</math> during the early 1950s. [[Paul Erdős]] proved that this bound is correct for <math>n</math>, a prime number. The general problem remains unsolved, apart from the best-known lower bound <math>\Omega((\log n)/n^2)</math> (achievable; hence, [[Heilbronn]]'s conjecture is not correct for general <math>n</math>) and upper bound <math>\exp(c \sqrt{\log n})/n^{8/7}</math> (proven by Komlos, Pintsz and Szemerédi in 1982 and 1981, respectively). Using the incompressibility method, the average case was studied. It was proven that if the area is too small (or large) it can be compressed below the Kolmogorov complexity of a uniformly-random arrangement (high Kolmogorov complexity). This proves that for the overwhelming majority of the arrangements (and the expectation), the area of the smallest triangle formed by three of <math>n</math> points thrown uniformly at random in the unit square is <math>\Theta(1/n^3)</math>. In this case, the incompressibility method proves the lower and upper bounds of the property involved.<ref>T. Jiang, M. Li, P. M. B. Vitanyi, "The average‐case area of Heilbronn‐type triangles", ''Random Structures & Algorithms'', 20:2(2002),  206–219. {{doi|10.1002/rsa.10024}}</ref>

===Probability===
The [[law of the iterated logarithm]], the [[law of large numbers]] and the recurrence property were shown to hold using the incompressibility method<ref>V. G. Vovk, "The law of the iterated logarithm for random Kolmogorov, or chaotic, sequences", ''Theory Probab. Appl.'' 3:32(1988), 413–426. {{doi|10.1137/1132061}}</ref> and [[Kolmogorov's zero–one law]],<ref>M. Zimand, "A high-low Kolmogorov complexity law equivalent to the 0–1 law", ''Inform. Process. Letters'', 57:2(1996), 59–84. {{doi|10.1016/0020-0190(95)00201-4}}</ref> with [[normal number]]s expressed as binary strings (in the sense of [[E. Borel]]) and the distribution of 0s and 1s in binary strings of high Kolmogorov complexity.<ref>M. Li, P. M. B. Vitanyi, "Statistical properties of finite sequences with high Kolmogorov complexity",  ''Mathematical Systems Theory'', 27(1994), 365–376. {{doi|10.1007/BF01192146}}</ref>

===<span class="anchor" id="Turing machines time complexity"></span>Turing-machine time complexity===
The basic Turing machine, as conceived by [[Alan Turing]] in 1936, consists of a memory: a tape of potentially-infinite cells on which a symbol can be written and a finite control, with a read-write head attached, which scans a cell on the tape. At each step, the read-write head can change the symbol in the cell being scanned and move one cell left, right, or not at all according to instruction from the finite control. Turing machines with two tape symbols may be considered for convenience, but this is not essential.

In 1968, F. C. Hennie showed that such a Turing machine requires order <math>n^2</math> to recognize the language of binary palindromes in the [[Best, worst and average case|worst case]]. In 1977, W. J. Paul<ref name="Pa"/> presented an incompressibility proof which showed that order <math>n^2</math> time is required in the average case. For every integer <math>n</math>, consider all words of that length. For convenience, consider words with the middle third of the word consisting of 0s. The accepting Turing machine ends with an accept state on the left (the beginning of the tape). A Turing-machine computation of a given word gives for each location (the boundary between adjacent cells) a sequence of crossings from left to right and right to left, each crossing in a particular state of the finite control. Positions in the middle third of a candidate word all have a [[Crossing sequence (Turing machines)|crossing sequence]] of length <math>O(n)</math> (with a total computation time of <math>O(n^2)</math>), or some position has a crossing sequence of <math>o(n)</math>. In the latter case, the word (if it is a [[palindrome]]) can be identified by that crossing sequence.

If other palindromes (ending in an accepting state on the left) have the same crossing sequence, the word (consisting of a prefix up to the position of the involved crossing sequence) of the original palindrome [[Concatenation (mathematics)|concatenated]] with a suffix the remaining length of the other palindrome would be accepted as well. Taking the palindrome of <math>\Omega(n)</math>, the [[Kolmogorov complexity]] described by <math>o(n)</math> bits is a contradiction.

Since the overwhelming majority of binary palindromes have a high Kolmogorov complexity, this gives a lower bound on the average-case [[Time complexity|running time]]. The result is much more difficult, and shows that Turing machines with <math>k+1</math> work tapes are more powerful than those with <math>k</math> work tapes in [[real-time computing|real time]] (here one symbol per step).<ref name="PSS"/>

In 1984, W. Maass<ref name="Ma">W. Maass, "Combinatorial lower bound arguments for deterministic and nondeterministic Turing machines", ''Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.'' 292 (1985), 675–693. {{doi|10.1090/S0002-9947-1985-0808746-4}}</ref> and [[Ming Li|M. Li]] and  [[Paul Vitányi|P. M. B. Vitanyi]]<ref name="LVa">M. Li, P. M. B. Vitanyi, "Tape versus queue and stacks: The lower bounds", ''Information and Computation'', 78:1(1988), 56–85. {{doi|10.1016/0890-5401(88)90003-X}}</ref> showed that the simulation of two work tapes by one work tape of a Turing machine takes <math>\Theta(n^2)</math> time [[Deterministic algorithm|deterministically]] (optimally, solving a 30-year [[open problem]]) and <math>\Omega (n^2/(\log n \log \log n))</math> time nondeterministically <ref name = "LVa"/> (in,<ref name="Ma" /> this is <math>\Omega (n^2/(\log^2 n \log \log n))</math>. More results concerning tapes, [[Stack (abstract data type)|stacks]] and [[Queue (abstract data type)|queues]], deterministically and nondeterministically,<ref name="LVa"/> were proven with the incompressibility method.<ref name="LV"/>

===Theory of computation===
[[Heapsort]] is a sorting method, invented by J. W. J. Williams and refined by [[R. W. Floyd]], which always runs in <math>O(n \log n)</math> time. It is questionable whether Floyd's method is better than Williams' on average, although it is better in the worst case. Using the incompressibility method, it was shown<ref name="LV"/> that Williams' method runs on average in <math>2n \log n +O(n)</math> time and Floyd's method runs on average in <math>n\log n+O(n)</math> time. The proof was suggested by [[Ian Munro (computer scientist)|Ian Munro]].

[[Shellsort]], discovered by [[Donald Shell]] in 1959, is a [[comparison sort]] which divides a list to be sorted into sublists and sorts them separately. The sorted sublists are then merged, reconstituting a partially-sorted list. This process repeats a number of times (the number of passes). The difficulty of analyzing the complexity of the sorting process is that it depends on the number <math>n</math> of keys to be sorted, on the number <math>p</math> of passes and the increments governing the scattering in each pass; the sublist is the list of keys which are the increment parameter apart. Although this sorting method inspired a large number of papers, only the worst case was established. For the average running time, only the best case for a two-pass Shellsort<ref>D. E. Knuth, ''Sorting and Searching'' (Vol. 3 ''The Art of Computer Programming''), 2nd Ed. Addison-Wesley, 1998, pp 83–95. {{ISBN|0201896850}}</ref> and an upper bound of <math>O(n^{23/15})</math> <ref>S. Janson, D. E. Knuth, "Shellsort with three increments", ''Random Structures Algorithms'' 10:1–2(1997), 125–142. {{arXiv|cs/9608105}}</ref> for a particular increment sequence for three-pass Shellsort were established. A general lower bound on an average <math>p</math>-pass Shellsort was given<ref name="JLV">T. Jiang, M. Li, P. M. B. Vitanyi, "A lower bound on the average-case complexity of Shellsort", ''Journal of the ACM (JACM)'', 47:5(2000) 905–911. {{doi|10.1145/355483.355488}}</ref> which was the first advance in this problem in four decades. In every pass, the comparison sort moves a key to another place a certain distance (a path length). All these path lengths are [[Logarithmic number system|logarithmically coded]] for length in the correct order (of passes and keys). This allows the reconstruction of the unsorted list from the sorted list. If the unsorted list is incompressible (or nearly so), since the sorted list has near-zero Kolmogorov complexity (and the path lengths together give a certain code length) the sum must be at least as large as the Kolmogorov complexity of the original list. The sum of the path lengths corresponds to the running time, and the running time is lower-bounded in this argument by <math>\Omega (pn^{1+1/p})</math>. This was improved to a lower bound of 
:<math>
\Omega \left( n\sum_{k=1}^p h_{k-1}/h_k \right)
</math>
where <math>h_0=n</math>.<ref>P.M.B. Vitanyi (2018), On the average‐case complexity of Shellsort, Random Structures and Algorithms, 52:2, 354–363 {{doi|10.1002/rsa.20737}}</ref> This implies for example the Jiang-Li-Vitanyi lower bound for all <math>p</math>-pass increment sequences and improves that lower bound for particular increment sequences;
the Janson-Knuth upper bound is matched by a lower bound for the used increment sequence, showing that three pass Shellsort for this increment sequence uses <math>\Theta(n^{23/15})</math> inversions.

Another example is as follows. <math>n,r,s</math> are natural numbers and <math>2 \log n \leq r,s \leq n/4</math>, it was shown that for every <math>n</math> there is a [[Logical matrix|Boolean]] <math>n \times n</math> matrix; every <math>s \times (n-r)</math> submatrix has a [[Matrix rank|rank]] at least <math>n/2</math> by the incompressibility method.

===Logic===
According to [[Gödel's incompleteness theorems|Gödel's first incompleteness theorem]], in every formal system with computably enumerable theorems (or proofs) strong enough to contain [[Peano arithmetic]], there are true (but unprovable) statements or theorems. This is proved by the incompressibility method; every formal system <math>F</math> can be described finitely (for example, in <math>f</math> bits). In such a formal system, we can express <math>K(x) \geq |x|</math> since it contains arithmetic. Given <math>F</math> and a natural number <math>n \gg f</math>, we can search exhaustively for a proof that some string <math>y</math> of length <math>n</math> satisfies <math>K(y) \geq n</math>. In this way, we obtain the first such string; <math>K(y) \leq \log n+f</math>: contradiction.<ref>[https://www.amazon.com/Algorithmic-Information-Cambridge-Theoretical-Computer/dp/0521616042 G. J. Chaitin, ''Algorithmic Information Theory'', Cambridge University Press, 1977.]</ref>

==Comparison with other methods==
Although the [[probabilistic method]] generally shows the existence of an object with a certain property in a class, the incompressibility method tends to show that the overwhelming majority of objects in the class (the average, or the expectation) have that property. It is sometimes easy to turn a probabilistic proof into an incompressibility proof or vice versa. In some cases, it is difficult or impossible to turn a proof by incompressibility into a probabilistic (or counting proof). In virtually all the cases of Turing-machine time complexity cited above, the incompressibility method solved problems which had been open for decades; no other proofs are known. Sometimes a proof by incompressibility can be turned into a proof by counting, as happened in the case of the general lower bound on the running time of [[Shellsort]].<ref name="JLV"/>
